sources.news_title: US inflation stubbornly high in challenge to Trump
sources.text:
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, the department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said in a statement, beating market expectations.
“The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports,” the BEA said in a statement.
The US Federal Reserve’s preferred gauge for inflation — the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index — rose by 3.6% year-on-year in September, an increase from the previous month.
Trump’s handling of the economy is a key issue for voters heading into midterm elections on Tuesday, where Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from the president’s Republican Party.
The US-Israel war on Iran has sent global energy prices skyrocketing due to Tehran’s retaliatory action, with US consumers paying an average of 42% more at the pump for regular gasoline, according to data from the AAA motor club.
The president’s wide-ranging tariff policies have also upended global trade and fuelled inflation.
Strong GDP growth
The strong GDP growth will come as a boon to Trump, who has touted the strength of the economy despite the high prices that have posed a challenge to households across the country.
Much of the economic growth has been driven by an investment boom in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, which has seen companies spend billions on new models and in building the data centres that power them.
The BEA said the acceleration in GDP growth was driven by an increase in investment and an upturn in government spending, which were partially offset by a decrease in exports.
Imports — which are a subtraction in the formula for GDP — also increased more in the third quarter than the previous one.
Thursday’s GDP data was an advance estimate released by the BEA, with two further estimates due in the coming weeks that could see the number revised.
Economists have warned for months that while US GDP growth has remained resilient despite price pressures from the war, outcomes have been highly uneven, with wealthier households prospering while working class families struggle.
Fed implications
The Fed prefers to use the PCE price index when gauging inflation, as it takes into account a broader range of household expenditures than Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation.
On Wednesday, the US central bank voted to keep interest rates steady, citing the need for more data to gauge how best to battle the surging inflation.
Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated the Fed’s commitment to its long-term two-percent target for PCE inflation, which it has not achieved for more than five years.
He termed current inflation levels “too high” but cautioned against moving too quickly, saying the Fed had seen some tightening of financial conditions in response to the Fed raising interest rates in September — its first hike in three years.
Markets largely expect the Fed to raise rates again by a quarter-point in December.
‘Failed agenda’
Trump’s political opponents slammed his handling of the economy over the quickening PCE figure, which showed a 21.3% year-on-year increase in the prices of energy goods and services.
“Today’s data confirms families paid more in September for gasoline, housing, and health care,” said Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren.
“Since Trump took office, families have paid US$3,772 on average because of inflation. Trump’s failed agenda is driving up costs and eating into Americans’ paychecks.”
At a rally in South Carolina, Trump boasted about the “roaring” economy, renewed his attacks on Fed officials over monetary policy and told supporters to stick to voting Republican.
“If the Democrats win the midterms, they will burn it all down,” he said.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said the US economy was “on steroids right now” but that high inflation was its “Achilles heel.”
“Growth came in stronger than expected and it’s largely due to the massive AI business investment surge,” she said. “The AI boom is adding almost a full percentage point to growth.”
Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said spending by consumers was still high, but “they are increasingly stretching their budgets to afford pricier goods and services.”

sources.news_title: Economy Is Running Hot on Strong Consumer Spending Growth & Massive AI Investment Boom

But the trade deficit worsened, driven by the AI boom. And the drunken sailors in Washington pushed the Debt-to-GDP ratio to 121.7%.
By Wolf Richter for WOLF STREET.
The overall economy, adjusted for inflation, grew by a strong 3.4% in Q3 annualized, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis today. A purer measure of the domestic private portion of the overall economy, also released by the BEA today, was red hot.
The private economy is red hot. The “Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchasers” excludes government spending, imports and exports, and the change in inventories. It reflects private-sector domestic demand and covers 88% of overall GDP.
This Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchases soared by 4.9% in Q3 annualized, adjusted for inflation, the fastest growth since the reopening of the economy in Q2 2021, after the already very strong growth rate in Q2 (+4.6%), according to the BEA today. So for a moment, forget the jump in government spending, forget imports and exports, forget the confusing inventory adjustment. This is the private US economy, and it’s hot.
“Real” GDP overall grew by 3.4%, adjusted for inflation, dragged down by a massive spike in imports (deducted from GDP) due to high-dollar AI data-center related equipment. The trade deficit knocked 3.32 percentage points off GDP growth.
In the years between the Great Recession and the pandemic (so excluding recessions), average quarter-to-quarter GDP growth was 2.5% annual rate. The average 20-year quarter-to-quarter GDP growth, including recessions, was 2.2% annual rate. So Q3 growth of 3.4% was far above average, despite the huge trade deficit.
How much each major component of GDP contributed to or subtracted from this 3.4% GDP growth, in percentage points:
- Consumer spending: +2.52
- Gross domestic private investment: +3.27
- Net Exports (trade deficit): -3.32
- Federal Government: +0.91
- State & Local governments: -0.1
“Current-dollar GDP” (not adjusted for inflation) grew by 5.6% to $33.0 trillion in “current dollars,” all annual rates.
This “nominal GDP” of $33.0 trillion represents the actual size of the US economy in today’s dollars and forms the basis for the Debt-to-GDP ratio (more in a moment) and similar GDP-based ratios.
The difference between this growth rate of 5.6% in current dollars, and the growth rate of “real” GDP of 3.4% was the rate of inflation in the overall economy in Q3 of 2.2%, the so-called GDP deflator. Average energy prices in Q3 dropped off from the horrendous spike in Q2, which helped reduce the GDP deflator in Q3.
Consumer spending jumped by an annual rate of 3.8% in Q3, adjusted for inflation, after having already jumped by 3.8% in Q2. That’s two quarters back-to-back of very strong consumer spending growth. Consumer spending accounted for 69% of the US economy.
This growth rate added 2.5 percentage points to the GDP growth of 3.4%.
The spending growth was spread over goods and services. All are adjusted for price changes (inflation):
- Services: +4.1%.
- Durable goods: +2.3%
- Nondurable goods: +3.4%.
The blue columns show the growth rates (left axis), the red line shows the dollars (right axis), all in seasonally adjusted annual rates (SAAR):
Gross private domestic investment (which includes change in private inventory inventory) spiked by 19.4% in Q3 annualized, to $4.8 trillion, adjusted for inflation.
This added 3.7 percentage points to the 3.4% GDP growth. This 19.4% spike was huge.
But part of it were purchases of AI related equipment, some of which ended up as inventory in warehouses, so the “change in private inventories” was huge and it’s included in gross private fixed investment here. That change in private inventory added 1.61 percentage points to the 3.4% GDP growth, as part of the 3.7 percentage points that gross private fixed investments added.
Private fixed investment, which excludes the confusing change in inventories, spiked by 9.4% in Q3 annualized, adjusted for inflation, after having already jumped by 7.7% in Q2 and by 6.1% in Q1.
It added 1.66 percentage points to 3.4% GDP growth.
This boom was driven at least in part by the AI investment boom.
But the component of “residential fixed investment” dropped in Q3, as the housing market faces a glut of new single-family and multifamily homes, and homebuilders and multifamily developers are applying some prudence to this housing glut (see my analysis: What the “Housing Shortage” of New Single-Family Homes Looks Like: Ballooning Inventories, Falling Prices, So-So Sales):
- Nonresidential fixed investments: +12.7%; that’s where the AI investment boom shows up.
  - Structures: +5.4%
  - Equipment: +20.9%, driven by AI equipment
  - Intellectual property products (software, movies, etc.): +8.4%.
- Residential fixed investment: -3.3%, driven by homebuilders and multifamily developers being prudent as they face a housing glut.
Private fixed investment accounted for 19% of the US economy.
Government consumption expenditures and gross investment spiked by 5.3% annualized, adjusted for inflation, after declining in Q2.
Note: This measure, “government consumption expenditures and gross investment,” does not include interest payments as interest payments are generally not included in GDP. And it does not include transfer payments made directly to consumers (the biggest part of which are Social Security payments), which are counted in GDP when consumers and businesses spend these funds or invest them in fixed investments.
Federal government spending spiked by 15.8% annualized in Q3, after the drop in Q2:
- National defense: +11.7%
- Nondefense: +22.2% after the -12.7% plunged in Q2
Federal government spending added 0.91 percentage points to 3.4% GDP growth.
State and local government spending declined by 0.1%, which subtracted 0.1 percentage points from GDP growth.
Combined, federal, state, and local government consumption and investment accounted for 20% of the US economy. About 60% of this measure of government spending is from state and local governments. Federal government spending accounts for about 40%.
Trade Deficit worsens on spiking imports of AI equipment.
“Net exports” (exports minus imports) worsened dramatically to an inflation-adjusted trade deficit of $1.32 trillion.
Net exports subtracted 3.32 percentage points from 3.4% GDP growth.
Imports spiked by 19.7% in Q3 annualized, adjusted for price changes, on spiking imports of high-dollar electronic products, including semiconductors to be used in AI data centers.
Imports are a negative in GDP, and this spike in imports deducted 2.64 percentage points from the 3.4% GDP growth.
- Imports of goods: +26.4%, a massive spike!
- Imports of services: -4.2% (includes US tourists spending overseas).
Exports plunged by 5.7%, after jumping in the prior two quarters. Exports are a positive in GDP. But the plunge (negative figure) subtracted 0.68 per percentage points from the 3.4% GDP growth.
- Exports of goods: -0.57%.
- Exports of services: -0.1% (includes foreign tourists spending in the US).
The Government’s Treasury Debt-to-GDP ratio ticked up to 121.7%, as current-dollar GDP rose 1.37% quarter-to-quarter not annualized to $33.0 trillion (see above), while the Treasury debt spiked by 1.8% quarter-to-quarter to $40.2 trillion.
So in Q3, the economy grew more slowly than the debt, and the Debt-to-GDP Ratio worsened, more than wiping out the improvement in Q2, but it’s lower year-over-year (down from 122.4% in Q3 2025).

sources.news_title: White House: Economy grows at 3.4% rate in third quarter as investment surges
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, the strongest pace in a year, the White House said Thursday, crediting President Donald Trump’s policies for driving investment and consumer spending that outpaced forecasts.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis reported the advance estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product earlier Thursday, showing growth accelerated from a 2.2% rate in the second quarter. Increases in investment, consumer spending and government spending contributed to the gain, partly offset by a decrease in exports and a rise in imports, according to the agency.
The White House said the figures show Trump’s America First agenda is delivering as promised: faster growth, historic levels of investment, and an economy that continues to outperform the so-called experts.
Private investment in plants and equipment rose at a 9.4% rate in the third quarter, accelerating from the second quarter, the White House said. Business investment overall grew nearly 13%, which the administration described as the strongest quarter in nearly 15 years. So far this year, investment is expanding more than twice as fast as in 2025 and three times faster than the 2.3% rate in the final year of the Biden administration, according to the White House.
Consumer spending increased at a 3.8% rate last quarter, the White House said, citing resilience among American households. Over the past three quarters, the economy has grown at a 2.7% rate, faster than the Blue Chip consensus forecast of 2.4% and the Congressional Budget Office’s projection of 2.2%, the statement said.
The White House noted that 72% of economists surveyed by Bloomberg underestimated the third-quarter growth figure. It also said capital goods now make up a record share of U.S. imports while consumer goods account for just 17% of goods imports, tied for the lowest level on record. Combined with the rise in domestic investment, the administration said this reflects policies aimed at rebuilding American productive capacity.
“President Trump’s agenda of lower taxes, fewer regulations, energy dominance, and America First trade are fueling a historic investment boom that is powering strong growth,” the White House said. “Businesses are betting on America, and the foundation of the future is being built right here at home.”
The BEA’s advance estimate is subject to revision. The agency is scheduled to release its second estimate of third-quarter GDP on Nov. 25.

sources.news_title: Economist: Strong GDP growth, inflation complicate Fed's decisions
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – The U.S. economy's strongest quarterly growth of 2026, coupled with stubborn inflation, could make interest rate decisions more difficult for the Federal Reserve in the months ahead, an economist told The Center Square.
“Accelerating growth amid persistent inflation is going to complicate the Federal Reserve's already complicated policy picture,” said Peter Earle, senior director of research for the American Institute for Economic Research.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis released its advance estimate for third-quarter GDP Thursday, reporting an annualized increase in real GDP of 3.4%.
Annual inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, increased to 3.6% in September from 3.4% in August, remaining well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target.
Investment increased in the third quarter, led by inventory and equipment purchases, particularly computers and related technology. Business investment in equipment rose 20.9% at an annualized rate, while investment in intellectual property products also increased.
Consumer spending grew at an annualized rate of 3.8%, matching the second quarter's pace, reflecting increases in both goods and services, including health care, food services and prescription drugs.
Although consumer spending continued to support economic growth, the acceleration from the second quarter was driven largely by stronger investment and a rebound in government spending, according to the BEA. The increase in government spending partly reflected fewer sales of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Because those sales are subtracted from government spending when calculating GDP, fewer sales resulted in a higher spending figure.
Imports, which count against GDP growth, increased for the third consecutive quarter in 2026, after declining through much of 2025. Exports, which contribute to GDP growth when they increase, declined in the third quarter after rising during the first half of the year.
“The headline growth number is impressive, but the underlying strength is more significant,” Earle said.
Earle pointed to both overall GDP growth and real final sales to private domestic purchasers, a measure of consumer spending and private fixed investment that excludes government spending, trade and inventory changes. The latter rose 4.9% in the third quarter, which Earle said “strongly suggest[s] genuine underlying economic momentum” rather than growth driven by more volatile components of the economy. He also noted continued growth in consumer spending.
While Earle emphasized that artificial intelligence is playing a major role in economic growth, he cautioned that spending on AI does not necessarily translate into equivalent economic returns and that much of the equipment used is imported, meaning not all of that spending contributes to U.S. economic output.
“It's important, especially watching growing concerns in stock and debt markets, to note that the economic benefits of technological innovation and the financial returns earned by its initial investors are two different matters with different implications,” Earle said.
Ryan Young, a senior economist at the Competitive Enterprise Institute, also sounded a cautionary note about AI.
“A lot of that growth is concentrated in AI. Much of the rest of the economy is growing more slowly than average. If there is an AI bubble and it pops, there could easily be a recession,” Young told The Center Square.
And while consumer spending continued to support economic growth, Young underscored that inflation has eroded consumers' purchasing power.
“Even though people are spending more, they are also getting less for their money due to the Iran war raising energy prices, and tariffs raising countless other prices,” Young said.

U.S. Economy Surges 3.4% in Third Quarter, Beating Expectations as Consumer Spending and Investment Accelerate
by Emmitt Barry, Worthy News Washington D.C. Bureau Chief
(Worthy News) – The U.S. economy expanded at a stronger-than-expected 3.4% annualized rate during the third quarter of 2026, accelerating sharply from 2.2% in the previous quarter as consumer spending and business investment fueled growth despite persistent inflation and rising energy costs.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis reported Thursday that gross domestic product (GDP) exceeded economists’ forecasts of approximately 3.2%, providing an encouraging sign of economic resilience under President Donald Trump’s administration.
Consumer spending, the largest component of the American economy, increased 3.8%, while business investment surged as companies poured billions into artificial intelligence infrastructure, computer equipment, and data centers.
Investment in business equipment climbed nearly 21%, helping drive the economy’s strongest quarterly expansion in a year.
Strong Growth Despite Inflation Pressures
The encouraging economic figures arrive as American households continue struggling with elevated gasoline prices, inflation, and borrowing costs.
Although economic growth accelerated, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge remained at 3.6% annually in September, considerably above the central bank’s 2% target.
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to maintain its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4%, citing continued inflation concerns despite strengthening economic activity.
The latest GDP figures also arrive just days before the November 3 midterm elections, giving the Trump administration a significant economic achievement to highlight as Republicans seek to maintain control of Congress.
Nevertheless, economists caution that rising energy costs, sluggish hiring, and persistent inflation could challenge the expansion heading into 2027.
The Commerce Department is scheduled to release its revised third-quarter GDP estimate on November 25.

sources.news_title: Strong GDP Growth Continues to Exceed Expectations in 3rd Quarter
sources.text:
The nation’s real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) continued to outperform economists’ predictions in the third quarter, a report released Thursday by the U.S. Commerce Department reveals.
Real (seasonally-adjusted) GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4% in the third quarter (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate published Thursday. That’s up from the second quarter’s 2.2% growth and the fastest pace in a year. The third quarter’s GDP growth also exceeded economists’ prediction of 3.1%.
Both the Commerce Department and economists have tended to underestimate real GDP increases in recent quarters.
In September, for example, the Commerce Department had to upwardly revise both its second quarter and first quarter measures of GDP growth, which exceeded economists’ expectations. In that report, real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment was revised up 0.4 percentage point from the previous estimate of 4.2%, which had been revised up from a prior estimate of 3.9%.
The third quarter’s GDP growth is greater than the second quarter’s 2.2% increase and the fastest rate since the third quarter of 2025. The main contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were consumer spending, investment, and government spending.
Consumer spending grew 3.8% in the third quarter, matching the second quarter’s growth – and remaining at the fastest pace since the fourth quarter of 2024. Consumer spending accounts for more than two-thirds of the nation’s economic output,
Those additions to GDP were partly offset by a decrease in exports and an increase in imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP. The drop in exports primarily reflected a decrease in goods (led by petroleum and related products), while the largest contributor to imports was capital goods, other than automotive.
The primary contributors to the increase in private inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing (both led by nondurable goods industries).
The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both goods and services:
- Within services, the increase was led by health care (mainly hospitals and outpatient services), food services and accommodations (mainly purchased meals and beverages).
- Within goods, the increase was led by other nondurable goods (particularly prescription drugs).
Total government spending rose at a 5.3% annualized rate in the third quarter. Here, federal government expenditures jumped 15.8%, while state and local spending dipped 0.1%%. The federal government increase was boosted by a 22.2% rise in nondefense consumption.
“The U.S. economy is on steroids right now,” thanks to higher-then-expected GDP growth, Navy Federal Credit Union Chief Economist Heather Long told The Hill. And, while inflation remains a concern, the economy is being largely fueled by “the massive AI business investment surge,” Long noted.

sources.news_title: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
sources.text:
Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
Summary
The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4 percent annualized rate in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year, as consumers spent robustly and businesses increased investment in AI-related equipment. Consumer spending rose 3.8 percent, while equipment investment surged 20.9 percent. Imports and rising inflation weighed on the outlook, and economists said the data strengthened the case for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.
Key Facts
- The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis said third-quarter GDP growth was the fastest since the third quarter of 2025, exceeding economists’ 3.2 percent forecast.
- Business equipment spending added 1.16 percentage points to GDP growth, while investment in intellectual property products increased at an 8.4 percent rate.
- Imports rose at a 19.7 percent rate and subtracted 2.64 percentage points from GDP growth; inventory rebuilding contributed 1.61 percentage points.
- The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index rose 3.6 percent year over year in September, while core PCE inflation increased 3.1 percent.
- Inflation-adjusted household income fell 0.3 percent in September, and inflation-adjusted consumer spending was unchanged that month.
WASHINGTON — The U.S. economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, shrugging off higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East as consumers maintained robust spending and businesses doubled down on investment in AI.
The better-than-expected increase in gross domestic product last quarter reported by the Commerce Department on Thursday was in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and deterioration in consumer sentiment.
The advance GDP report was published less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Economists said the strong growth, together with other data on Thursday showing inflation accelerating and broadening out in September, bolstered the argument for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December.
The U.S. central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75 percent-4.00 percent range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."
"The consequences of an economy at full employment in addition to a historic capital expenditures expansion are on vivid display," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "If the Fed is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending ... stratospheric private non-residential investment and sizzling inflation data."
Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4 percent annualized rate last quarter, the quickest since the third quarter of 2025, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its first estimate of third-quarter GDP. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2 percent pace.
The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Fed officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2 percent.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8 percent rate in the July-September period, matching the second quarter's pace. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation. Households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending.
Business spending on equipment surged at a 20.9 percent rate, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020. That added 1.16 percentage points to GDP growth, the most in six years. Business spending on intellectual property products grew at an 8.4 percent rate, contributing just under half a percentage point to GDP growth.

The strong GDP growth will come as a boon to Trump, who has touted the strength of the economy despite the high prices that have posed a challenge to households across the country.

The Fed prefers to use the PCE price index when gauging inflation, as it takes into account a broader range of household expenditures than Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — The U.S. economy grew at a stronger-than-expected annual rate of 3.4% during the third quarter, accelerating from the previous three months as businesses increased investment and American consumers continued spending despite elevated inflation and borrowing costs.
Gross domestic product, the broadest measure of economic activity, increased at a seasonally and inflation-adjusted annual rate of 3.4% from July through September, according to the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis report released Thursday.
The expansion exceeded economists’ expectations of 3.1% growth and represented a substantial acceleration from the second quarter’s 2.2% increase.
The report showed that business investment, household spending and government expenditures contributed to economic growth, partially offset by weaker exports and rising imports.
One of the strongest indicators was real final sales to private domestic purchasers, a measure of underlying demand that excludes government spending, inventories and net exports.
That measure increased at a 4.9% annualized rate, compared with 4.6% in the second quarter, reaching its fastest pace since the second quarter of 2021.
The acceleration suggests that demand from American households and private businesses remained strong even as the Federal Reserve maintained interest rates at levels intended to restrain inflation.
Consumer spending, which accounts for approximately two-thirds of U.S. economic activity, grew at a 3.8% annual rate.
That matched the previous quarter’s increase and exceeded economists’ expectations of 3.5% growth.
The continued expansion in household spending helped support economic activity despite concerns about higher prices, financing costs and slowing employment gains.
Business investment also contributed substantially to the stronger GDP reading.
Companies increased spending on equipment, particularly computers and information-processing technology, while businesses also accumulated inventories at a faster pace.
Investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, including computing equipment and data centers, has helped sustain demand for technology and related capital equipment.
According to the Commerce Department, the investment increase reflected stronger private inventory accumulation and equipment purchases, particularly in wholesale trade, manufacturing and information technology.
Government spending also increased during the quarter, reversing its previous decline and adding to overall economic growth.
However, part of the measured increase reflected changes in federal transactions involving oil held in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
A reduction in government sales of reserve oil altered the accounting treatment of federal spending without representing an equivalent increase in government purchases or direct economic activity.
International trade, meanwhile, weighed on the overall GDP figure.
Imports increased during the third quarter, subtracting from the GDP calculation, while exports declined.
The increase in imported goods partly reflected demand for equipment and other products used by American businesses.
Under national income accounting rules, imports are subtracted because they represent goods and services produced outside the United States. Their increase does not necessarily indicate weaker domestic demand.
The report also provided updated inflation figures.
The price index for gross domestic purchases increased at a 3.0% annual rate, compared with 5.6% during the second quarter.
The personal consumption expenditures price index, an important inflation measure monitored by the Federal Reserve, increased at a 2.1% annualized quarterly rate, compared with 5.0% previously.
Excluding volatile food and energy prices, the PCE price index increased at a 2.5% rate, down from 3.3% in the preceding quarter.
Those quarterly inflation measurements indicate slower price increases during the July-through-September period, although they do not mean consumer prices returned to earlier levels.
The GDP figures arrive one day after the Federal Reserve voted to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4%.
Federal Reserve officials cited resilient domestic spending, strong productivity growth and robust capital investment in their assessment of the economy.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the central bank said in its Wednesday policy statement, while warning that inflation remained elevated.
The combination of stronger economic growth and persistent inflation presents a challenge for policymakers deciding whether additional interest rate increases are necessary.
Higher borrowing costs can reduce demand and help contain inflation, but they can also discourage business investment, residential construction and consumer purchases.
The latest GDP figures indicate that private demand remained strong through September despite those pressures.
The report was released less than a week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when the economy, inflation and household affordability remain prominent issues.
Although GDP measures total economic production, it does not directly establish whether household purchasing power or living standards have improved equally across income groups.
Strong overall economic growth can coexist with financial pressure on families facing rising housing, food, energy or other expenses.
Thursday’s release represents the government’s advance estimate of third-quarter GDP, meaning the figures remain subject to revision as additional economic data become available.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis is scheduled to publish its second estimate Nov. 25, incorporating more complete information on consumer spending, investment, trade and government expenditures.
For now, the report shows that the U.S. economy entered the final quarter of 2026 with stronger growth than economists anticipated, supported by continued consumer spending and a substantial expansion in private domestic demand.

Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 3.2% growth, and the gain was the quickest since the third quarter of 2025, Reuters reported. It was the last major economic report before Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, rose at a 3.8% rate, matching the prior quarter. Business spending on equipment surged 20.9%, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020.
Much of that spending went to imports, which climbed at a 19.7% rate and subtracted 2.64 percentage points from growth. Government spending rose 5.3%, while higher mortgage rates pushed residential investment back into contraction.
“Consumption was still strong. But business investment is turbocharging the U.S. economy,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote on X. Charles Schwab strategist Liz Ann Sonders noted the AI build-out “is very import-driven.”
President Donald Trump welcomed the numbers before heading to a campaign rally. “We had a great morning from the standpoint of GDP,” he told reporters. The White House hailed the report on X as a major boost for the economy.

The monthly jump was the largest since March and was driven largely by energy, CNBC reported. Gasoline and other energy goods rose 9.2% in September alone.
Household budgets felt the squeeze. Inflation-adjusted disposable income fell 0.3% in September, and inflation-adjusted consumer spending was unchanged. The personal saving rate stood at 3.8%.
Gas prices remain about $1 a gallon higher than a year ago as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran drags on, The Guardian reported. The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index is down 15% since February.

“Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs,” said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.

sources.text:
Robust business investment and resilient consumer spending drove stronger-than-expected economic growth in the third quarter.
Gross domestic product, the value of all goods and services produced across the economy, rose at a seasonally and inflation-adjusted 3.4 percent annual rate from July through September, the Commerce Department said Thursday.

Imports, which are a subtraction from GDP, rose in the third quarter.

Private nonresidential fixed investment, a key measure of business activity, grew at a 12.7 percent rate, the swiftest pace since the the third quarter of 2020. Within that, investment in business structures grew at a 5.4 percent rate. Investment in business equipment grew at a 20.9 percent rate, the fastest pace since the pandemic rebound in the third quarter of 2020. The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Commerce Department’s measure of inflation, rose at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 2.1 percent. Core PCE prices, which exclude food and energy, rose at a 2.5 percent pace.
Nominal GDP, which is not adjusted for inflation, expanded at an annualized 5.6 percent rate.

By Alicia Wallace, Elisabeth Buchwald, CNN
(CNN) — US economic growth accelerated last quarter at its fastest pace in a year; however, rising gas prices helped to lift inflation in September to a four-month high, new data showed Thursday.
The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index rose 0.5% from August, bringing the annual rate of inflation to 3.6% from 3.4%, according to new Commerce Department data, well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% inflation target.
Thursday’s inflation data was in line with economists’ expectations and echoed the trends seen in the September Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index reports, which showed inflation remaining stubbornly high because of a war-driven energy shock as well as other price pressures.
Excluding food and gas, categories that tend to be volatile, the core PCE price index rose 0.3% from August, lifting the annual rate to 3.1% from 3%.
The PCE price index is part of the Commerce Department’s monthly Personal Income and Outlays report, which includes comprehensive data on how Americans earn, spend and save.
Americans pumped the brakes on their spending last month, the report also showed. Consumer spending rose 0.5%, slowing from a gain of 0.9% the month before. When adjusting for inflation, consumer spending was flat from the month before.
Consumer spending has held up despite broader economic shocks – including a war-driven spike in energy costs – but it has come partly at the expense of savings as income growth has slowed. Thursday’s report showed that the personal savings rate (savings as a percentage of after-tax income) fell 0.2 percentage points to 3.8%, the lowest rate in nearly four years.
Personal income grew 0.2% from August, slowing from a rate of 0.3%. However, US households are taking home less: Inflation-adjusted after-tax income fell 0.3% from September, Commerce Department data shows.
“It’s easy to talk on the aggregate and say the consumer is really holding the economy aloft, and in many ways they are, but that’s not uniform across households,” said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360 and former senior economist at NerdWallet. “Obviously, some households are going to feel a lot more stress from the higher inflation than others.”
A stronger case for Fed hike
Separately on Thursday, the Commerce Department reported that US economic growth accelerated during the third quarter, with gross domestic product expanding at a 3.4% inflation-adjusted annualized rate, a faster pace than the 3.0% rate economists had projected. GDP captures the value of all goods and services across the economy.
Last month, the central bank raised rates for the first time in three years. But the rate increase has yet to slow business investment as companies looked to build up more AI-related infrastructure last quarter. Business investment skyrocketed last quarter to an annualized pace of 12.7% from 9% in the prior quarter.
US consumers also played a large part in boosting the economy, with spending remaining at a robust 3.8% annualized pace. Consumer spending accounts for more than two thirds of US GDP.
But US economic growth would have been even higher had exports not declined by 5.7% last quarter. In calculating GDP, the government factors in the value of total exports minus total imports.
That means that when the value of exports exceeds that of imports, it helps lift overall GDP. And last quarter there was an especially large gap between the two, with imports surging to a nearly 20% annualized pace, a likely reflection of businesses stockpiling ahead of Canadian tariffs taking effect, combined with data center-related purchases.
Still, the past quarter’s strong growth story gives the Fed more of a runway to combat rising prices by increasing interest rates by at least a quarter point at its next monetary policy meeting in December.

“The AI boom and the irrepressible American consumer are keeping the economy from cooling, even as monetary policy becomes more restrictive,” said Olu Sonola, head of US economics at Fitch Ratings. “The Fed is tightening the screws, but the economy has yet to get the memo. Strong growth and inflation paints mixed picture of economy days before midterm elections
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. economic growth was notably strong from July to September, yet inflation accelerated at the same time, new data showed Thursday, painting a mixed picture about the country’s economy less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living looms larger than perhaps any other issue.
Strong consumer spending and soaring investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure were key drivers of growth in the third quarter. When unemployment is as low as it is right now, consumers often spend at a healthy clip and they are doing so, particularly wealthier Americans who are riding a wave of record stock market gains.
The economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, the Commerce Department said Thursday, much faster than the 2.2% growth in the April-June quarter.
Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth and far exceeding the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Business investment, driven by spending on AI infrastructure, jumped 12.7%, the most in six years.
How long can this economic growth continue?
Yet economists worry that persistently high prices are eroding Americans’ ability to keep up. Thursday’s data suggest consumers are increasingly dipping into savings to cover their costs. After-tax incomes, adjusted for inflation, slipped from August to September and were up just 1% from a year earlier. At the same time, inflation-adjusted spending rose 2.5% from a year earlier.
As Americans splurged, the savings rate fell to 3.8% in September, its lowest level in four years, data published Thursday showed.
“High energy prices are chipping away at purchasing power,” Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote. “Real income failed to grow for a second consecutive month, while the saving rate continued to decline. Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters.”
Inflation worsens
Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May.
Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of the energy sector. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched.
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. was $4.23 on Thursday, 39% more than it cost a year ago. Diesel prices have risen much faster. While most consumers don’t buy diesel, it has an outsized impact on inflation because it is used in industrial sectors and shipping.

The Commerce Department on Thursday reported that the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index rose 0.5% on a monthly basis in September and was up 3.6% from a year ago. Both figures were in line with the expectations of economists polled by LSEG.

Compared with August's readings, headline PCE ticked up from 3.4% to 3.6%, while core PCE rose from 3% to 3.1%.
Goods prices were up 3.9% year over year, while services prices increased 3.5% from a year ago in September.
The personal savings rate as a percentage of disposable personal income was 3.8%, down from 4% in August. Over the last two years, the savings rate has declined from a peak of 6.2% in April 2025 and from 5.6% in January 2026.
While inflation moved further away from the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also released the advance estimate for third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP), which grew more than expected.

WHITE HOUSE ECONOMIC CHIEF REVEALS WHY AMERICANS AREN'T FEELING OPTIMISTIC ABOUT ECONOMY

The monthly increase was the largest since March, but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below, CNBC reported.
Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, CNBC noted that officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends.
Inflation Ahead of Target
While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed’s 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter.
GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter.
Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%, the Commerce Department said.
Despite elevated inflation readings, Fed officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move.

More Work To Do

Initial jobless claims moved lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s, CNBC noted.

With gasoline still above $4 a gallon as the war between the US, Israel and Iran drags on, a slowdown in spending looks likely in the months ahead.

sources.news_title: US Economy Surges As AI Investment Fuels 3.4% Growth
sources.text:
US Economy Surges as AI Investment Fuels 3.4% Growth
The US economy growth defied expectations by expanding at a robust 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter of 2026, its fastest pace in a year. The report, released Thursday by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), indicated strong consumer spending and a significant surge in business investment, particularly in artificial intelligence technology.
This acceleration, up from 2.2% in the second quarter, paints a picture of an economy with surprising momentum, pushing back against persistent forecasts of a slowdown. The figure comfortably beat projections from economists at FactSet, Bloomberg, and Reuters, which had centered around 3.2%. This resilience arrives amidst wider market concerns and geopolitical developments creating global economic shifts.
Economy surges on consumer spending and AI
The primary engine of the third quarter’s performance was the American consumer. Household spending increased at a swift 3.8% annual rate, continuing a trend that has puzzled economists. This resilience suggests a strong labor market and wage gains are providing a solid foundation for spending.
“The seemingly indefatigable US consumer and a nascent AI investment boom continue to drive the US economy, with growth running well above trend,” said James McCann, a senior economist at Edward Jones. This sentiment underscores the core drivers of the current expansion.
Beyond the consumer, the report’s most striking component was a massive jump in business investment. Overall private fixed investment leaped 9.4%, the largest increase since the post-pandemic rebound of 2020. This indicates that companies are confident enough to commit significant capital to expansion and upgrades.
The data reveals a specific focus on technology, pointing to an “AI investment boom.” Business investment excluding housing soared by 12.7%, with spending on information processing equipment skyrocketing by a massive 37.4%. Investment in software also posted a strong 9.6% gain, reflecting a broad-based push by corporations to integrate new technologies. This commitment to tech sector growth underscores the strategic importance of digital transformation.
A closer look at the components of GDP growth
While consumer and business spending were the stars, other factors contributed to the headline number. Federal government spending increased at a 15.8% rate, partly reflecting oil sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. This provided a significant, though likely temporary, boost to the overall GDP calculation.
However, not all sectors shared in the boom. The housing market remains a notable weak spot, with investment dropping 3.3% as high mortgage rates continue to choke off activity. This was the sixth quarterly decline in the last seven quarters for the sector.
It’s highly sensitive to the Federal Reserve’s interest rate policy and broader bond market moves, with the 10-year Treasury yield recently touching 5.00%.
The report also highlighted a significant drag from international trade. A surge in imports, which rose at a 19.7% rate, subtracted 2.64 percentage points from GDP. In national accounting, imports are treated as a negative because they represent domestic demand being met by foreign production. Falling exports subtracted another 0.68 points.
This dynamic presents a complex picture. “It looks like a strong quarter driven by domestic demand activities and a drag from trade,” noted Eric Winograd, Senior Economist for Fixed Income at AllianceBernstein.
“We talk about the boost to growth from AI, but a lot of that stuff is imported,” he added, highlighting that the tech boom is fueling demand for hardware often produced overseas, reflecting global supply dynamics for components.
Mixed signals from the inflation front
For officials at the Federal Reserve, the GDP report contains a mix of encouraging and complicating data points on inflation. The headline news on this front was positive: the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, rose at a much slower 2.1% rate in the third quarter. This is a significant deceleration from the 5.0% rate seen in Q2.
This slowing in the quarterly price index suggests that the Fed’s aggressive rate-hiking campaign is having its intended effect. It’s cooling price pressures across the economy. A sustained trend in this direction would give the central bank more confidence that it is on track to return inflation to its 2% target.
But more recent monthly data included in the report offers a note of caution. Consumer prices in September rose 3.6% from a year earlier, and core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy, also saw a slight uptick. This persistence in monthly inflation, combined with strong overall growth, could make the Fed hesitant to signal an end to its tightening cycle.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh acknowledged the economy’s vigor, stating that “economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.” He noted that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” He also pointed to “healthy” consumer spending and high levels of capital expenditures.
What this means for the economic outlook
The surprisingly strong third-quarter performance fundamentally resets the short-term economic narrative. Fears of an imminent recession, which dominated discussions for much of the past year, have now been largely pushed aside. This momentum raises questions about its sustainability.
The data shows an economy that has so far absorbed the highest interest rates in decades with remarkable ease. The key question for the fourth quarter and beyond is whether this strength can last. Some economists wonder if consumers are running down pandemic-era savings to fuel their spending, a finite source of funds.
The durability of the AI investment cycle is another unknown; it’s unclear if it is a temporary surge or the beginning of a longer-term productivity-enhancing trend. Significant headwinds remain. Geopolitical instability, particularly the war in Iran, has pushed U.S. oil prices back above $100 a barrel.
This could translate to higher gasoline prices and dampen consumer sentiment. And borrowing costs remain high for both consumers and businesses. These factors will continue to act as a brake on economic activity, especially in rate-sensitive sectors like housing and auto sales.
Ultimately, the report complicates the path forward for the Federal Reserve. While slowing quarterly inflation is welcome news, the sheer strength of the underlying economy suggests the fight against inflation may not be over. Policymakers will be watching incoming data on the labor market and inflation very closely as they weigh their next move.
The economy has proven more resilient than anyone expected, but its future trajectory remains far from certain.

sources.news_title: US economy beats growth forecasts as September inflation rises to 3.6%
sources.text:
- US GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, beating economists’ forecast of 3.1%.
- The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.6% year over year in September, while core inflation stood at 3.1%.
- Strong investment, resilient consumer spending and low jobless claims are complicating the Federal Reserve’s efforts to bring inflation back to target.
The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, even as inflation accelerated in September, presenting the Federal Reserve with a difficult balance between controlling prices and sustaining economic momentum.
Gross domestic product increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 3.4% in the July-to-September period, according to Commerce Department data released Thursday. That exceeded economists’ expectations of 3.1% and marked an acceleration from the 2.2% growth recorded in the second quarter.
At the same time, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, rose 0.5% in September from the previous month. The annual inflation rate reached 3.6%, remaining well above the central bank’s 2% target.
Excluding food and energy, core PCE inflation increased 0.3% month over month and 3.1% year over year. The core measure is closely watched by policymakers because it can provide a clearer indication of underlying price pressures.
The figures followed the Fed’s decision Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%. Officials have signaled that they want to assess incoming economic data before deciding on their next move.
“The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that’s happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said.
The latest reports suggest that policymakers may have limited room to ease monetary policy while inflation remains elevated and economic activity continues to expand.
What is driving US economic growth?
Consumer spending and business investment remained major contributors to growth in the third quarter.
Consumer spending increased 3.8%, matching the pace recorded in the previous quarter. Gross private domestic investment surged 19.4%, supported by a 20.9% increase in equipment spending and an 8.4% rise in investment in intellectual property products.
Spending linked to the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure has helped support investment, alongside continued consumer and government expenditure.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, a measure of underlying private-sector demand closely watched by Fed officials, rose 4.9%, up from 4.6% in the second quarter.
Personal income, however, increased by a more modest 0.2% in September, below economists’ forecast of 0.3%. Consumer spending rose 0.5% during the month, slightly short of the expected 0.6%.
The labor market also showed resilience. Initial claims for unemployment benefits fell to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 in the week ending October 24, below economists’ expectations of 200,000. The reading pointed to continued low levels of layoffs.
The combination of steady household spending, strong investment and relatively limited job losses suggests that the economy has maintained momentum despite elevated borrowing costs and persistent inflation.
Why are inflation and interest rates still a concern?
Energy costs were a major contributor to September’s price increases. Gasoline and other energy goods rose 9.2% during the month, while energy goods and services overall increased 5.4%.
Economists are concerned that higher energy costs could feed into other parts of the economy, including transportation, production and household services. Services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4% in September, while housing costs increased 0.3%.
There was some encouraging news in the quarterly figures. Headline PCE prices rose at a 2.1% annualized rate in the third quarter, down from 5% in the second quarter. Core PCE prices increased at a 2.5% pace, compared with 3.3% previously.
However, the September figures indicate that monthly price pressures remain substantial, with energy costs adding to the challenge.
Financial markets reacted to the data, with stock futures moving lower and Treasury yields falling following the releases.
For the Federal Reserve, the central question is whether inflation will ease without a significant slowdown in economic activity. Strong growth and low layoffs reduce the immediate pressure to support the economy through lower interest rates, while rising prices argue for caution.
The latest figures do not determine the Fed’s next decision, but they reinforce the uncertainty surrounding the path of monetary policy. If energy prices continue to rise or spread into broader costs, policymakers could face a more prolonged period of restrictive interest rates. If inflation moderates while growth remains firm, the central bank would have more room to assess its options.
For now, the US economy is demonstrating resilience, but the combination of above-target inflation and strong demand means the path toward lower inflation remains uncertain.

sources.news_title: Ahead of midterms: US economy posts strong growth, inflation stubbornly high in challenge to Trump
sources.text:
The United States posted strong economic growth in the third quarter, but the Fed's preferred inflation gauge also accelerated, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, in a mixed economic bag for US President Donald Trump ahead of key midterm polls next week.
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the department's Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said in a statement, beating market expectations.
"The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports," the BEA said in a statement.
The US Federal Reserve's preferred gauge for inflation -- the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index -- rose by 3.6 percent year-on-year in September, an increase from the previous month.
Trump's handling of the economy is a key issue for voters heading into midterm elections on Tuesday, where Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from the president's Republican Party.
The US-Israel war on Iran has sent global energy prices skyrocketing due to Tehran's retaliatory action, with US consumers paying an average of 42 percent more at the pump for regular gasoline, according to data from the AAA motor club.
The president's wide-ranging tariff policies have also upended global trade and fueled inflation.
The strong GDP growth will come as a boon to Trump, who has touted the strength of the economy despite the high prices that have posed a challenge to households across the country.
Much of the economic growth has been driven by an investment boom in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, which has seen companies spend billions on new models and in building the data centers that power them.
The BEA said the acceleration in GDP growth was driven by an increase in investment and an upturn in government spending, which were partially offset by a decrease in exports.
Imports -- which are a subtraction in the formula for GDP -- also increased more in the third quarter than the previous one.
Thursday's GDP data was an advance estimate released by the BEA, with two further estimates due in the coming weeks that could see the number revised.
Economists have warned for months that while US GDP growth has remained resilient despite price pressures from the war, outcomes have been highly uneven, with wealthier households prospering while working class families struggle.
The Fed prefers to use the PCE price index when gauging inflation, as it takes into account a broader range of household expenditures than Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation.
On Wednesday, the US central bank voted to keep interest rates steady, citing the need for more data to gauge how best to battle the surging inflation.
Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to its long-term two-percent target for PCE inflation, which it has not achieved for more than five years.
He termed current inflation levels "too high" but cautioned against moving too quickly, saying the Fed had seen some tightening of financial conditions in response to the Fed raising interest rates in September -- its first hike in three years.
Markets largely expect the Fed to raise rates again by a quarter-point in December.
Trump's political opponents slammed his handling of the economy over the quickening PCE figure, which showed a 21.3 percent year-on-year increase in the prices of energy goods and services.
"Today's data confirms families paid more in September for gasoline, housing, and health care," said Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren.
"Since Trump took office, families have paid $3,772 on average because of inflation. Trump's failed agenda is driving up costs and eating into Americans' paychecks."
At a rally in South Carolina, Trump boasted about the "roaring" economy, renewed his attacks on Fed officials over monetary policy and told supporters to stick to voting Republican.
"If the Democrats win the midterms, they will burn it all down," he said.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said the US economy was "on steroids right now" but that high inflation was its "Achilles heel."
"Growth came in stronger than expected and it's largely due to the massive AI business investment surge," she said. "The AI boom is adding almost a full percentage point to growth."
Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said spending by consumers was still high, but "they are increasingly stretching their budgets to afford pricier goods and services."

U.S. Core PCE Inflation Rises 3.1% as December Fed Hike Risk Draws Focus
Overall PCE inflation rose 3.6% year over year, while markets are watching whether service prices climb further.
Elevated U.S. inflation in September kept a possible December Federal Reserve rate increase in market focus, with core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) prices rising 3.1% from a year earlier.
The overall PCE price index increased 3.6% year over year. The headline measure includes food and energy, while the core reading removes both, leaving separate views of broad and underlying price growth. Both figures track changes over a 12-month period, not a single month.
Rising energy prices drove the headline rebound as international oil prices climbed amid Middle East conflict. Markets are also watching whether businesses pass higher fuel costs on to consumers.
Core PCE is the Fed's most closely watched inflation gauge. Its services component reflects whether domestic price pressures are persisting, keeping that category central to market expectations.
If service prices rise further, markets could put greater odds on a 25-basis-point increase at the Fed's December policy meeting.

sources.news_title: Fed's preferred inflation measure comes in hot at 3.6%
sources.text:
- Key insight: The September Personal Consumer Expenditure inflation rate came in at 3.6%, a number that in itself is unlikely to shape the Fed's next policy decision but it adds another key data point for the central bank to consider.
- Expert quote: "The information we receive over the coming period, will help us determine where we want policy to be, and at every turn, good or bad, our job is to get monetary policy right, and that's exactly what we're doing." —Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh
The latest print from the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation indicates the central bank still has work to do on price stability.
The personal consumption expenditures, or PCE, index from the Bureau of Economic Analysis was released Thursday morning and shows that prices rose by 0.5% month over month and 3.6% year over year in September.
Both marks were above the August PCE readings of 0.3% on the month and 3.4% on the year. Core inflation in September, which factors out food and energy prices, rose 3.1% — well above the Fed's 2% target. The report showed that gasoline and other energy goods represented the largest portion of increased monthly consumer spending, while motor vehicles and parts showed the biggest declines in monthly spending in September.
The results were largely expected after two previous inflation readings — the consumer price index and producer price index, both from the Bureau of Labor Statistics — already showed higher-than-expected price growth last month.
The September report also mirrors consensus market forecasts, which predicted an annualized reading of 3.7% overall inflation and 3.1% core.
The latest PCE reading comes one day after the Federal Open Market Committee voted to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged while it awaits more data about the trajectory of the U.S. economy and the impact of its quarter-point interest rate hike in September.
In addition to arriving too late to influence the FOMC's October decision, the reading also likely arrives too early to have much bearing on the committee's next interest rate decision in December.
Still, it adds another data point for the Fed to consider as it tracks the development of the inflation situation and weighs its next option.
"The information we receive over the coming period, will help us determine where we want policy to be, and at every turn, good or bad, our job is to get monetary policy right, and that's exactly what we're doing," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said during his post-FOMC press conference on Wednesday.
Read more:

- UMB says deal gives it access to wealth fleeing California
- CFPB flunks cybersecurity audit amid staff cuts: OIG report
- BofA adds Wisconsin to branch map, with more states to come
Before the next FOMC meeting, scheduled for Dec. 9 and 10, the Fed is set to receive employment reports from October and November as well as a full slate of inflation readings — CPI, PPI and PCE — from October.
The Fed will also have a fuller picture of how the overall economy is performing. The BLS' advanced estimate for third-quarter gross domestic product growth was also released on Thursday morning, showing a 3.4% annualized growth rate.
During his press conference, Warsh said the committee goal is to keep inflation in check without dampening the strong growth of the overall economy.
"The goal, in my view … isn't to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work. I don't think we have to do that," Warsh said, noting that the Fed is merely looking to tighten monetary policy enough to ensure it is not overly accommodative. "[Conditions have] tightened a bit since we met last time. That isn't something that we're uncomfortable with. That tells me the policy is working, and I think we can do that and make the economy more durable, have it last longer, and still achieve stable prices."

sources.news_title: US GDP Accelerates to 3.4% as Consumer Spending and Investment Drive Growth - ActionForex
sources.text:
US economic growth accelerated from 2.2% to 3.4% annualized in Q3, exceeding market expectations of 3.2%, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis’ advance estimate. The stronger expansion was driven by increases in private investment, consumer spending and government spending, partly offset by weaker exports and higher imports. Compared with Q2, the acceleration primarily reflected stronger investment and an upturn in government spending, while trade provided a larger drag. The report highlighted continued resilience in domestic economic activity, despite the negative contribution from net exports.
Investment was a major driver of the acceleration, led by increases in private inventories and equipment spending. Inventory accumulation was concentrated in wholesale trade and manufacturing, particularly nondurable goods industries. Meanwhile, equipment investment was led by information-processing equipment, mainly computers and peripheral equipment. The strength was consistent with September’s advance trade report, which showed capital goods imports jumping 7.5%, or approximately $10.9B. However, the increase in imported capital goods also contributed to the negative trade balance, illustrating how stronger investment demand can coincide with a drag from net exports. The BEA identified petroleum and related products as the main source of declining exports, while capital goods led the increase in imports.
Consumer spending also continued expanding across goods and services. Services growth was led by health care, particularly hospitals and outpatient services, alongside restaurants and accommodations. Among goods, prescription drugs were an important contributor. More significantly, real final sales to private domestic purchasers accelerated from 4.6% to 4.9% annualized, indicating that underlying private demand remained strong even excluding inventories, net exports and government spending. The improvement suggests that Q3’s robust expansion was not solely dependent on inventory accumulation, with household consumption and private fixed investment providing substantial support.
The stronger growth performance was accompanied by a moderation in quarterly inflation. The annualized PCE price index slowed from 5.0% to 2.1%, while core PCE inflation eased from 3.3% to 2.5%. The gross domestic purchases price index also moderated from 5.6% to 3.0%. Together, the figures suggest that resilient economic activity coincided with slower quarterly price increases, although they do not establish that inflation pressures have been fully contained. The separately released September PCE figures will provide a more detailed assessment of price developments at the end of the quarter. Overall, the GDP report points to strong underlying domestic demand alongside easing quarterly inflation, offering a more balanced economic picture than the headline growth surprise alone.
Data Summary

| Indicator | Q2 | Q3 | 
|---|---|---|
| Real GDP Growth (Annualized) | 2.2% | 3.4% | 
| Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchasers | 4.6% | 4.9% | 
| Current-Dollar GDP Growth (Annualized) | — | 5.6% | 
| Gross Domestic Purchases Price Index | 5.6% | 3.0% | 
| PCE Price Index (Annualized) | 5.0% | 2.1% | 
| Core PCE Price Index (Annualized) | 3.3% | 2.5% | 
Headline consensus: 3.2%, compared with actual GDP growth of 3.4%, representing a 0.2 percentage-point upside surprise.
Main Contributors to Growth
| Component | Q3 Development | 
|---|---|
| Private Investment | Increased, led by inventories and equipment | 
| Consumer Spending | Increased across goods and services | 
| Government Spending | Increased, partly reflecting federal nondefense spending | 
| Exports | Decreased, led by petroleum and related products | 
| Imports | Increased, led by capital goods, excluding automotive | 
Notable investment detail: Information-processing equipment, particularly computers and peripheral equipment, led the increase in equipment investment.
Source: US Bureau of Economic Analysis, GDP Advance Estimate, Q3 2026, released October 29, 2026. Growth and quarterly inflation figures are seasonally adjusted annualized rates.
Key Takeaways
- US GDP growth accelerates above expectations: Real GDP increased from 2.2% to 3.4% annualized in Q3, exceeding the 3.2% consensus. Investment, consumer spending and government spending supported expansion, while trade detracted.
- Investment drives much of the acceleration: Stronger private inventory accumulation and equipment investment were key contributors. Inventories increased in wholesale trade and manufacturing, while information-processing equipment led capital spending growth.
- Private domestic demand remains resilient: Real final sales to private domestic purchasers accelerated from 4.6% to 4.9%, indicating that underlying household consumption and private fixed investment remained strong beyond inventory accumulation.
- Consumer spending expands across goods and services: Health care, restaurants and accommodations supported services spending, while prescription drugs contributed to goods consumption.
- Trade provides a significant offset: Exports declined, particularly petroleum and related products, while imports increased, led by capital goods. The pattern is consistent with September’s sharp increase in capital goods imports.
- Investment and import growth occur together: Strong demand for imported equipment supports business capital expenditure but also contributes to the negative net export component of GDP. The increase should not be interpreted as purely domestic production growth.
- Quarterly inflation moderates despite stronger growth: Annualized headline PCE inflation slowed from 5.0% to 2.1%, while core PCE eased from 3.3% to 2.5%. The gross domestic purchases price index also moderated from 5.6% to 3.0%.
- Growth-inflation picture becomes more balanced: The economy maintained strong domestic momentum while quarterly price increases slowed. However, the advance estimate does not establish that inflation persistence has been resolved, and September’s separate PCE figures require independent assessment.

Tomorrow’s preliminary estimate of third-quarter GDP is expected to show a strong acceleration in U.S. economic activity from the second quarter, underscoring the economy’s resilience despite elevated interest rates and persistent geopolitical uncertainty. While stronger growth is a positive signal for corporate earnings and labor market conditions, it could also complicate the inflation outlook.
A stronger-than-expected GDP reading could reinforce concerns that underlying price pressures remain sticky while raising expectations for near-term Federal Reserve rate hikes. With those issues in mind, investors will be closely watching the Federal Reserve today, which is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged.
That leaves Fed Chairman Warsh facing a delicate balancing act at today’s press conference, where he will likely be pressed on the decision to hold rates steady despite his comment last month that “the plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.”
Earlier this month Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said “Inflation remains above our goal,” but “We have some time to wait and see how financial conditions evolve before we take more action.”
Meanwhile, tomorrow’s Q3 GDP report still appears set to show a solid pickup in growth, based on the median estimate for a set of nowcasts compiled by The Capital Spectator. Output is projected to increase at a 3.3% annualized pace during the July-through-September period, a notable improvement from Q2’s 2.2% gain.
This week’s release of September data for the Chicago Fed National Activity Index (CFNAI) supports the case for anticipating a roughly 3% GDP growth in the third quarter. Based on 85 indicators spanning production, employment, consumption, housing, and business activity, the index provides a broad, hard-data snapshot of the economy.
Third-quarter growth appears to have been driven by AI infrastructure spending, healthy consumer demand, and strong business investment in areas such as software and equipment. The details will matter as much as the headline number since broad-based gains in consumer and business spending would signal a healthier expansion than growth driven mainly by trade or inventory swings.
Even so, the headline GDP figure may overstate the economy’s underlying momentum. Investors should look beyond the top-line number, especially as real wages have softened and growth remains uneven across households and businesses.
Another key part of tomorrow’s report will be the inflation data embedded in the GDP release. A strong growth number combined with firmer-than-expected price pressures would reinforce concerns that inflation remains stubbornly elevated, complicating the Fed’s policy outlook. By contrast, solid growth alongside cooling inflation would strengthen the case that the economy can continue expanding without igniting a renewed inflation problem.
